opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most immediate and concrete risks we face from the current generation of AI, much more so than some of the science-fiction scenarios people like to talk about.

Here's the basic problem. Democracy depends on a shared sense of what's true. People can disagree about values and about policy, but if they can't agree on basic facts, if they can't trust what they read or see or hear, then the whole system of deliberation starts to break down. Large language models are, in effect, machines for producing plausible-sounding text at essentially zero marginal cost. They don't have any intrinsic connection to truth. They're very good at mimicry, at producing things that *sound* authoritative, and they're completely indifferent to whether what they're saying is accurate.

Now put that in the hands of bad actors: troll farms, state-sponsored influence operations, people who want to swing an election. It used to be that running a disinformation campaign took a lot of human labor. You needed people writing posts, making fake accounts, tailoring messages. Now you can generate thousands, millions of variations, customized to different audiences, in different languages and styles, almost for free. Add synthetic images, cloned voices, deepfake video, and you have a real scaling problem.

And there's a second-order effect that I worry about just as much, which is that once people know that anything could be fake, they start to distrust everything. That's sometimes called the "liar's dividend." A politician caught on tape doing something terrible can just say, "Oh, that's AI." So you get both a flood of fake content and an erosion of trust in real content. Both are corrosive.

What frustrates me is that we have very few safeguards in place. There's no robust requirement for watermarking or provenance, the detection tools aren't reliable, the platforms have cut back on trust and safety teams, and the regulatory response has been slow and fragmented. The companies building these systems have mostly said, "Trust us." I don't think that's good enough when what's at stake is the integrity of elections and the information ecosystem itself.

So to me this isn't hypothetical. It's here, it's cheap, and it's going to get worse unless we take it seriously: better regulation, real accountability for the companies, investment in detection and provenance, and frankly AI that's actually grounded in facts rather than just statistical patterns of words.

r001.rationale: The response mentions deepfake video and influence operations aimed at swinging an election, but it does not clearly say that deepfakes about political candidates could materially change an election’s outcome.

r002.rationale: It describes a flood of fake content that can make people distrust everything and lose confidence in what is real, conveying that propaganda can leave people unsure what to believe.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I've been worried about this for a long time, and I think the core of it is pretty simple. Democracy runs on a shared sense of what's true. It doesn't require everybody to agree, but it requires that we can at least argue from roughly the same set of facts. And large language models have, for the first time, made the production of plausible-sounding falsehood essentially free.

Think about what it used to cost to run a disinformation campaign. The Russians in 2016 had to hire actual humans in St. Petersburg to sit in an office and write posts. There was friction. There were limits on volume and on how well the writing could be tailored. Now you can generate ten thousand variations of a lie, each in fluent English or Spanish or Hindi, each tuned to a particular demographic, in an afternoon, for a few dollars. The marginal cost of a fake news story, or a fake persona, or a fake grassroots movement, has gone to roughly zero.

And the thing people sometimes miss is that these systems don't need to be good at telling the truth to be dangerous. They're actually terrible at that. They hallucinate constantly. But that's not a bug from the disinformation perspective. If your goal is to flood the zone, as Steve Bannon put it, you don't care whether any individual piece is accurate. You care that people can no longer tell the difference, that they get exhausted, that they give up on the idea that truth is knowable at all. That's the real damage. Not that people believe one specific lie, but that they stop believing anything.

I also think we should be honest about the fact that the companies building these tools have not been serious about this. I testified in the Senate about it, and I said then that we needed things like watermarking, provenance standards, some way of tracing where content came from. Very little has happened. The incentives all point the other way. And meanwhile the tools keep getting better at sounding human, at writing persuasively, at impersonating real people.

So when I say it's a threat to democracy, I don't mean it in a vague, hand-wavy way. I mean that the information ecosystem that elections depend on is being poisoned, cheaply and at scale, and we don't have the institutions in place to deal with it. That seems to me like a pretty urgent problem, and I don't think we should be waiting for a catastrophe to take it seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI-generated falsehoods and election-related information damage, but does not identify deepfakes about political candidates or say they could materially change an election’s outcome.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the strategy is to “flood the zone” so people cannot tell truth from falsehood, become exhausted, and stop believing anything.

astra-6.text:
Because democracy depends on people being able to make informed decisions, and automated disinformation makes it much easier to pollute the information they rely on. Propaganda is hardly new. What changes is the cost and the scale: you can generate enormous amounts of plausible-sounding text, tailor it to different audiences, and make one coordinated campaign look like thousands of independent voices.

These systems don’t have to be reliable to cause trouble. They just have to produce something persuasive enough that people share it. Checking a claim can take much longer than generating it, so there’s a fundamental asymmetry there.

And the danger isn’t only that people believe a particular falsehood. It’s that they stop knowing what to believe at all. If everything could be fabricated, people can dismiss genuine evidence, too. That undermines the shared factual basis we need to debate policy and hold people accountable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automated disinformation generally, but does not mention deepfakes about political candidates or say they could change an election outcome.

r002.rationale: It describes a flood of plausible content and coordinated voices, then says people may stop knowing what to believe, which captures the firehose strategy's stated effect.

sol-6.1.text:
Because democracy depends on people being able to make informed choices, and automated disinformation makes it much cheaper to undermine that. You can generate enormous amounts of plausible-sounding text without any commitment to whether it’s true, tailor it to different audiences, and keep producing variations indefinitely.

The danger isn’t just that someone believes a particular false story. It’s that the information environment becomes so polluted that people don’t know whom to trust. They may start to think that everything is propaganda and that there’s no point in trying to establish the facts. That makes democratic accountability much harder.

And there’s an asymmetry: generating a false claim can take seconds; checking it and getting the correction to everyone who saw it can take much longer. Automation amplifies that imbalance.
